edition.name: The mole people: life in the tunnels beneath New York City
edition.sourceProvenance: Frozen from the 1993 first-edition Open Library record, the Google Books work-family page, the Chicago Review Press product page, the CCLS Syndetics table of contents and professional reviews, later reporting recorded in manifests/source-ledger.json, and publisher-permitted listing excerpts used for narrow Chapter 1-6 support.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Below ground, people do not live in one generic dark place. The chapter names subway, railroad, and sewage tunnels so the underground starts to look like different survival settings instead of one blurry hiding space. That matters because different spaces create different pressures. They change movement, visibility, danger, and the chance of staying hidden. The chapter's strongest point is that place is not just background. It helps organize what kind of life is possible there.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The underground is not one uniform zone. The lawful summaries identify subway, railroad, and sewage tunnels, and those categories are enough to show that environment changes risk. A person in one kind of tunnel is not facing the same conditions as a person in another. The chapter treats space as a force shaping survival, not as scenery behind it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: The underground gets misread when people imagine one dark hole under the city. This chapter breaks that shortcut. Subway, railroad, and sewage tunnels are different pressure fields, not interchangeable hiding spots. Once that becomes clear, place stops being atmosphere and starts acting like part of the mechanism that structures danger and endurance.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter opens by refusing the blur. Underground life does not happen in one generic dark place. The lawful summaries explicitly name subway, railroad, and sewage tunnels, and that naming is enough to change the whole frame. Once the underground splits into different environment types, the reader has to stop imagining one shared condition and start thinking about different kinds of physical pressure.
chapterBreakdown.direct: That shift matters because space affects what daily survival feels like. Different tunnel types imply different movement patterns, access points, visibility levels, and exposure to danger. The chapter does not need a full engineering map to make that point. It only needs to show that environment changes what a hidden life demands from the people living inside it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: This is where place stops being scenery. If the setting changes how hidden you are, how quickly others can reach you, and how livable routine becomes, then the setting is part of the mechanism shaping the life. The chapter's discipline is to keep that claim narrow and real instead of drifting into guided-tour fiction.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Chapter 6 has to turn space into a force without pretending the lawful bundle supports a full geography. The authorized summaries name subway, railroad, and sewage tunnels, and that is enough to establish physical plurality below ground. Once the underground becomes plural, the chapter can argue that environment changes the conditions under which hidden life becomes possible, risky, and sustainable.
chapterBreakdown.direct: That move matters because place is never neutral at this scale. Different tunnel types imply different relations to movement, access, concealment, smell, noise, and interruption. The chapter does not need to fabricate route maps to make the point. It only needs to show that the physical setting changes what survival asks of a person and what kinds of social arrangements can take hold there.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: This is the point where setting stops behaving like atmosphere and starts behaving like mechanism. If the space changes how visible you are, how exposed you remain, and how repeatable your routines can become, then the space is already structuring the life. The previous chapter's population map therefore remains incomplete until place enters the analysis as an active pressure field.
chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter also has to keep concealment and danger in contact. Hidden space can reduce some topside exposure, but the official summaries do not allow a safe-refuge story. Danger remains above and below ground. The better claim is narrower: going underground changes the distribution of risk without abolishing risk itself. That is why physical hiding place and physical safety cannot be treated as synonyms.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Once that is clear, social life looks different too. Physical environments affect whether people can gather, remain alone, move frequently, stay hard to find, or build routines that hold for more than a moment. Space does not determine everything, but it helps set the range of what becomes workable. Population and environment therefore press on each other rather than existing as separate layers.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: The strongest reading refuses the guided-tour temptation. Because place is vivid, bad writing rushes toward cinematic detail the source bundle cannot justify. The disciplined chapter stops earlier. It maps environment types, shaping effects, and pressure differences. That restraint is not a weakness. It is what keeps the chapter honest enough to deepen the book without inventing the route it cannot lawfully see.

examples.title: Naomi Stops Treating the Setting as Background

scenario.gentle: Naomi is planning an outreach route with a transit map open on the table. She keeps describing the people she hopes to reach but not the environments they are moving through.
scenario.direct: An outreach planner notices that her notes track people well but flatten the physical settings shaping access and danger.
scenario.competitive: Naomi can keep talking about people in the abstract, or she can admit the route itself is part of the case.

whatToDo.gentle: Add the setting back into the analysis and ask how different spaces change visibility, access, and risk.
whatToDo.direct: Treat environment as part of the problem definition rather than as scenery.
whatToDo.competitive: If the space is changing the terms, put the space in the file.

whyItMatters.gentle: Behavior often looks different once the physical environment is taken seriously.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter teaches that place can quietly organize what a hidden life demands.
whyItMatters.competitive: Miss the pressure field and you misread the people inside it.

examples.title: Felix Revises a Clean Diagram of a Messy Space

scenario.gentle: In an urban-planning seminar, Felix looks at his wall diagram and realizes he turned all underground life into one undifferentiated zone.
scenario.direct: A student map simplifies the underground into one box and misses that different environments shape different pressures.
scenario.competitive: Felix built a neat slide out of a space problem that is not neat at all.

whatToDo.gentle: Rework the diagram so it shows environment types and the limits of what can be claimed.
whatToDo.direct: Split the setting into meaningful categories and keep the claims at category level.
whatToDo.competitive: Trade the fake clean picture for a narrower, truer one.

whyItMatters.gentle: A clean diagram can erase the material differences that shape real life.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter warns against letting one visual blur stand in for several pressure environments.
whyItMatters.competitive: If the map is too smooth, the room is already lying.

examples.title: Tori Hears Why Hiding and Safety Are Not the Same

scenario.gentle: Tori is talking with a relative who assumes that if a place is hidden, it must feel safer. She has to explain why concealment can still leave a life under severe pressure.
scenario.direct: A family conversation collapses hiddenness into safety, and Tori has to break that equation.
scenario.competitive: Tori is asked to accept cover as rescue and has to show why that math fails.

whatToDo.gentle: Separate concealment from safety and keep risk in the conversation.
whatToDo.direct: Explain that a hidden setting can reduce some exposure while preserving other dangers.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not let invisibility masquerade as protection.

whyItMatters.gentle: People often confuse being harder to see with being easier to live.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter keeps danger above and below ground in one frame for exactly this reason.
whyItMatters.competitive: Cover changes the fight. It does not end it.

examples.title: Julian Predicts the Cost of a Touristic Description

scenario.gentle: Julian reads a draft article that turns a hidden setting into a cinematic tunnel tour and senses that the vividness is outrunning the support.
scenario.direct: An editor spots geography getting more specific than the available evidence can justify.
scenario.competitive: Julian can publish fake exploration or force the draft back under source control.

whatToDo.gentle: Trim the route-writing and keep the description at the level of environment type and pressure.
whatToDo.direct: Replace scene-heavy geography with category-level claims the source posture can support.
whatToDo.competitive: Kill the tour and keep the map honest.

whyItMatters.gentle: Place becomes misleading fast when detail outruns support.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter's restraint is part of what keeps it trustworthy.
whyItMatters.competitive: Flashy routes are often just unsupported confidence in disguise.

examples.title: Miri Chooses Whether to Flatten Place for Clarity

scenario.gentle: In an after-school newsroom, Miri has a draft that would read more simply if all underground spaces were described as one zone.
scenario.direct: A student editor has to choose between easier prose and more accurate environmental distinctions.
scenario.competitive: Miri can flatten the place for speed or keep the harder truth that different spaces change different pressures.

whatToDo.gentle: Keep the distinctions that matter, even if the paragraph becomes slightly less simple.
whatToDo.direct: Preserve the environment categories and explain why they change the argument.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not buy clarity by selling off reality.

whyItMatters.gentle: Simple descriptions often erase the physical differences that shape real lives.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter shows that one-space language weakens both social and moral understanding.
whyItMatters.competitive: Flattening the setting flattens the people next.

examples.title: Seth Relearns What a Setting Can Do

scenario.gentle: Before, Seth thought of place as where life happens. After paying attention to how one cramped stairwell changes movement, noise, and privacy, he starts seeing environment differently.
scenario.direct: Seth shifts from treating setting as backdrop to treating it as an active force shaping behavior.
scenario.competitive: He learns that the room was doing more than hosting the action. It was helping script it.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask what a place is allowing, blocking, and pressuring at the same time.
whatToDo.direct: Look for how environment changes routine, exposure, and relation instead of only mood.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop reading the set as wallpaper and start reading it as leverage.

whyItMatters.gentle: Better spatial reading can change how people and problems are understood.
whyItMatters.direct: Chapter 6 offers a way to think about setting as one of the forces shaping a life.
whyItMatters.competitive: If place is part of the mechanism, ignoring it is a category mistake.
